commit_message:
[string] Optimize and refactor index hashing

gotos are considered harmful and switches are not, so extract out
helper functions from index hashing which report whether the index
contained non-index (non-digit or leading zero) values, or whether it
simply overflowed.

Also do some microoptimisation that merges the index check with the
conversion to decimal, and changes the overflow check to detect overflow
(with a single branch) rather than prevent it (with branches dependent
on both the current digit and the value so far). This should reduce
branches and tighten the loop.

findings.title: uint32_t overflow with unrecoverable undo in TryParseArrayIndex
findings.message: In `TryParseArrayIndex`, the `index` accumulator is declared as `uint32_t`. For 10-digit strings on 64-bit platforms, the loop expression `index = (10 * index) + val` can silently overflow a 32-bit integer. After the full loop, an overflow-detection block attempts to undo the last iteration via `index -= chars[i - 1]`. This undo is doubly wrong: (1) it subtracts the raw ASCII character value (e.g., 50 for '2') rather than the digit numeric value (e.g., 2), and (2) it does not account for the wrapping that occurred in the multiplication `10 * index`, which destroys information and is not reversible. As a concrete example, parsing '8589934640' causes `10 * 858993464 + 0 = 8589934640` to wrap to 48 (mod 2^32). The undo then computes `48 - '0' = 48 - 48 = 0`. When this corrupted zero is passed to `TryParseIntegerIndex`, the assertion `DCHECK_GT(index, 0)` at line 183 fires, crashing a debug build.

related_locations.description: DCHECK_GT(index, 0) fires when the corrupted (zero) index is passed in after the flawed undo
uint32_t& index parameter declaration — the root cause of the overflow on 64-bit platforms

findings.suggestion: Use a 64-bit accumulator on 64-bit platforms so the multiplication never overflows for values in the valid integer-index range. The fix introduces `using ArrayIndexT = uint64_t` on 64-bit hosts and `uint32_t` on 32-bit hosts, then uses `ArrayIndexT& index` throughout. On 64-bit, overflow detection reduces to a simple `if (index > String::kMaxArrayIndex) return kOverflow;` without any undo logic.

ground_truth.root_cause: The `index` variable was typed as `uint32_t` even on 64-bit platforms where integer indices can legitimately exceed 32-bit range before the overflow boundary is reached. When `10 * index` wraps a 32-bit integer, information is permanently lost; the subsequent subtraction-based undo cannot reconstruct the original value. The overflow detection condition (`index + 1 < kMinValidValue + 1`) also fails to catch all overflow cases where the wrapped result accidentally falls within the valid uint32_t range.
